title: ३५ लाख पुराना ग्राहकको इन्टरनेट शुल्क किन बढ्यो दोब्बर ? यसरी सम्भव छ सस्तो इन्टरनेट
content:
काठमाडौं । नेपालको इन्टरनेट सेवा क्षेत्रमा पछिल्लो समय भएको मूल्यवृद्धिले आम उपभोक्तामाथि गम्भीर आर्थिक भार थपेको छ। निजी इन्टरनेट सेवा प्रदायक (ISP) हरूले गत दसैँको समयमा शुल्कमा उल्लेख्य वृद्धि गरेपछि सर्वसाधारणमा असन्तुष्टि बढेको छ। तर, मूल्यवृद्धिको वास्तविक कारण के हो, त्यसको लागतसँग कति सम्बन्ध छ र उपभोक्तामाथि थपिएको आर्थिक भार कति हो भन्ने विषयमा सरकारले अहिलेसम्म प्रभावकारी जवाफ दिन सकेको छैन। निजी इन्टरनेट सेवा प्रदायकहरूको साझा संस्था ISPAN ले सार्वजनिक सूचना जारी गर्दै मूल्यवृद्धिको औचित्य पुष्टि गर्न अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय परिस्थितिलाई कारण देखाएको छ। विशेषगरी अमेरिका–इरान युद्ध, अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय बजारमा पेट्रोलियम पदार्थको मूल्यवृद्धि तथा फाइबर अप्टिक केबल, राउटर र अन्य दूरसञ्चार उपकरणको मूल्य बढेको भन्दै इन्टरनेट सेवाको शुल्क बढाउनुपरेको उसको तर्क छ। तर, यहाँ एउटा महत्वपूर्ण प्रश्न उठ्छ- नयाँ ग्राहक जडान गर्दा आवश्यक पर्ने राउटर, फाइबर केबल तथा अन्य उपकरणको मूल्य बढेको हो भने वर्षौंदेखि इन्टरनेट सेवा प्रयोग गरिरहेका पुराना ग्राहकको मासिक शुल्कसमेत किन एकैपटक बढाइयो? के अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय बजारमा पेट्रोलियम पदार्थ र फाइबर केबलको मूल्य बढ्दैमा पहिले नै जडान भइसकेका लाखौँ ग्राहकको इन्टरनेट सेवा सञ्चालन लागत पनि त्यही अनुपातमा बढ्छ? सरकारले निजी ISP हरूको यस्तो तर्कको प्राविधिक र आर्थिक आधार अध्ययन गरेको छ कि छैन? यी प्रश्नको जवाफ खोज्नु सरकार र नियामक निकायको प्रमुख जिम्मेवारी हो। ३५ लाख पुराना ग्राहकको शुल्क किन बढाइयो ? नेपाल दूरसञ्चार प्राधिकरण (NTA) का तथ्यांकअनुसार नेपालमा फिक्स्ड ब्रोडब्यान्ड इन्टरनेटका ग्राहक करिब ३५ लाखको हाराहारीमा छन्। यी ग्राहक वर्षौंदेखि विभिन्न निजी ISP का नेटवर्कमा जोडिएका छन्। उनीहरूको घर, कार्यालय तथा व्यावसायिक प्रतिष्ठानमा फाइबर अप्टिक ड्रप केबल जडान भइसकेको छ। आवश्यक राउटर तथा नेटवर्क उपकरण पनि उपलब्ध छन्। सडक किनारमा रहेका नेपाल टेलिकम तथा नेपाल विद्युत् प्राधिकरणका पोलमार्फत विस्तार गरिएका नेटवर्कबाट उनीहरूले नियमित इन्टरनेट सेवा लिइरहेका छन्। नयाँ ग्राहक थप्दा लाग्ने प्रारम्भिक जडान खर्च नयाँ ग्राहकसँगै उठाउनुपर्ने हो। तर, पहिले नै नेटवर्कमा जोडिएका ग्राहकलाई दिइने नियमित इन्टरनेट सेवाको शुल्कमा समेत त्यस्तो खर्च जोडेर उठाउनु कति न्यायोचित हो? यस विषयमा नियामक निकाय, सञ्चार तथा सूचना प्रविधि मन्त्रालय र नेपाल दूरसञ्चार प्राधिकरणको मौनताले आर्थिक अनियमितता र मिलेमतोको आशंकासमेत बढाएको छ। नयाँ ग्राहक जडान गर्दा राउटर, ड्रप केबल, कनेक्टर, जडान श्रम तथा अन्य उपकरणमा अतिरिक्त लगानी आवश्यक पर्न सक्छ। तर पुराना ग्राहकका हकमा ती उपकरण र जडान खर्च पहिले नै भइसकेका हुन्छन्। त्यसैले नयाँ उपकरणको मूल्य बढेको कारण देखाएर पुराना ग्राहकको मासिक सेवा शुल्कसमेत उल्लेख्य रूपमा बढाउनुको औचित्य के हो भन्ने प्रश्न स्वाभाविक हो। पुराना ग्राहकलाई सेवा निरन्तर उपलब्ध गराउँदा नेटवर्क मर्मत, विद्युत्, अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय ब्यान्डविथ, नेटवर्क विस्तार, कर्मचारी तथा अन्य सञ्चालन खर्च भने लागिरहन्छन्। तर ती खर्चमा कति वृद्धि भयो र त्यसले ग्राहकको मासिक शुल्कमा कति प्रभाव पार्नुपर्ने हो भन्ने कुरा तथ्यांकबाट प्रमाणित हुनुपर्छ। नयाँ ग्राहकको जडान खर्च र पुराना ग्राहकलाई उपलब्ध गराइने नियमित ब्यान्डविथ सेवाको शुल्कलाई एउटै डालोमा राखेर मूल्यवृद्धिको औचित्य पुष्टि गर्न सकिँदैन। नयाँ ग्राहकले उपकरणको विकल्प रोज्न पाउने व्यवस्था किन नगर्ने ? सरकारले तत्काल समाधानका रूपमा नयाँ जडान र नियमित इन्टरनेट सेवाको शुल्कलाई पारदर्शी रूपमा छुट्याउने व्यवस्था गर्न सक्छ। नयाँ ग्राहकले आवश्यकताअनुसार आधुनिक राउटर, फाइबर ड्रप केबल तथा अन्य उपकरण आफैँ खरिद गर्न चाहेमा त्यसको वास्तविक मूल्य छुट्टै तिर्न पाउने व्यवस्था गर्न सकिन्छ। ISP ले उपकरण उपलब्ध गराउने हो भने त्यसको मूल्य, गुणस्तर र स्वामित्वसम्बन्धी विवरण स्पष्ट हुनुपर्छ। त्यस्तै, पुराना ग्राहकका हकमा पहिले नै जडान भइसकेका उपकरण तथा पूर्वाधारको लागत पुनः नयाँ ग्राहकको जडान लागतसरह जोडेर शुल्क निर्धारण गरिएको छ कि छैन भन्ने अध्ययन हुनुपर्छ। सरकारले नियामकीय अध्ययनमार्फत पुराना ग्राहकको सेवा शुल्क र नयाँ जडानको उपकरण तथा पूर्वाधार शुल्कबीच उचित भिन्नता कायम गर्ने विकल्प तयार गर्न सक्छ। यसले नयाँ ग्राहकलाई उपकरण छनोट गर्ने स्वतन्त्रता दिनुका साथै पुराना ग्राहकलाई अनावश्यक आर्थिक भारबाट जोगाउन मद्दत पुर्‍याउन सक्छ। युद्ध र पेट्रोलियम मूल्यवृद्धिले इन्टरनेटको शुल्क कति बढाउँछ ? ISP हरूले अमेरिका–इरान युद्ध तथा अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय बजारमा पेट्रोलियम पदार्थको मूल्यवृद्धिलाई समेत शुल्क बढाउनुको कारणका रूपमा प्रस्तुत गरेका छन्। निश्चय पनि अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय युद्ध, इन्धनको मूल्यवृद्धि, ढुवानी खर्च, विदेशी मुद्रा विनिमय दर तथा उपकरणको मूल्यले दूरसञ्चार क्षेत्रको लागतमा प्रभाव पार्न सक्छ । तर त्यसको वास्तविक प्रभाव कति हो भन्ने प्रश्नको जवाफ अनुमानका आधारमा दिन मिल्दैन । उदाहरणका लागि, कुनै ISP ले पहिले नै खरिद गरेको फाइबर अप्टिक केबल, राउटर र अन्य उपकरण प्रयोग गरेर लाखौँ ग्राहकलाई सेवा दिइरहेको छ भने नयाँ उपकरणको अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय मूल्य बढ्दैमा सबै पुराना ग्राहकको मासिक इन्टरनेट शुल्क स्वतः दोब्बर हुनुपर्ने आधार हुँदैन । त्यसैगरी, अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय ब्यान्डविथ खरिदको मूल्य, विदेशी मुद्रा विनिमय दर, विद्युत्, नेटवर्क मर्मत तथा अन्य सञ्चालन खर्चमा भएको वास्तविक परिवर्तनको छुट्टाछुट्टै हिसाब हुनुपर्छ । सरकारले ISP हरूबाट विगत र वर्तमान लागतको तुलनात्मक विवरण मागेर अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय महँगीको वास्तविक प्रभाव सार्वजनिक गर्नुपर्छ । युद्धको प्रभाव कति, उपकरणको महँगी कति र वास्तविक सञ्चालन खर्च कति बढ्यो भन्ने प्रमाणित विवरणबिना आम उपभोक्तालाई मूल्यवृद्धिको भार बोकाउन मिल्दैन । १०० देखि ६०० Mbps का प्याकेज बेच्ने ISP को वास्तविक क्षमता कति ? नेपालको इन्टरनेट बजारमा विभिन्न सेवा प्रदायकले १००, २००, ३००, ४००, ६०० Mbps र त्यसभन्दा माथिका प्याकेज घोषणा गरेका छन्। तर नेपालमा इन्टरनेट सेवाको अधिकतम स्पिड ८८ Mbps मात्र रहेको दाबी लेखमा गरिएको छ। ISP हरूले स्थानीय भिडियो सामग्री तथा नेपालका विभिन्न स्थानमा जडित CDN Server मा संग्रहित डिजिटल सामग्रीलाई समेत अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय इन्टरनेट ब्यान्डविथका रूपमा प्रस्तुत गरेर शुल्क उठाइरहेको आरोप पनि उठाइएको छ। यस विषयमा सञ्चार तथा सूचना प्रविधि मन्त्रालय र नेपाल दूरसञ्चार प्राधिकरण किन मौन छन्? ग्राहकले मासिक, त्रैमासिक, अर्धवार्षिक तथा वार्षिक रूपमा शुल्क भुक्तानी गरिरहेका छन्। तर ग्राहकले खरिद गरेको इन्टरनेट प्याकेज र ISP ले वास्तवमा उपलब्ध गराउन सक्ने नेटवर्क क्षमताबीच कस्तो सम्बन्ध छ भन्ने विषय आम उपभोक्तालाई थाहा छैन। यहाँ अर्को महत्वपूर्ण प्राविधिक विषय आउँछ- Oversubscription Ratio। यसको अर्थ ISP ले आफ्नो नेटवर्कको कुल उपलब्ध क्षमताको तुलनामा कति ग्राहकलाई सेवा बिक्री गरेको छ भन्ने हो। सबै ग्राहकले एकै समयमा आफ्नो प्याकेजको अधिकतम गति प्रयोग गर्दैनन् भन्ने आधारमा नेटवर्क सञ्चालनको योजना बनाइन्छ। तर सरकारले प्रत्येक ISP को कुल खरिद गरिएको अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय ब्यान्डविथ, स्थानीय ट्राफिक, व्यस्त समयमा हुने वास्तविक प्रयोग र ग्राहकलाई बिक्री गरिएको क्षमताको तुलनात्मक अध्ययन गर्नुपर्छ । यदि कुनै ISP ले लाखौँ ग्राहकलाई विभिन्न उच्च गतिको प्याकेज बिक्री गरेको छ भने ती ग्राहकलाई सेवा दिन आवश्यक वास्तविक नेटवर्क क्षमता कति छ ? निष्कर्ष : डिजिटल नेपाल बनाउने हो भने इन्टरनेट जनताको पहुँचभन्दा बाहिर जान दिनु हुँदैन सरकारले डिजिटल नेपालको सपना देखिरहेको छ। तर डिजिटल नेपाल निर्माणको आधार मानिने इन्टरनेट नै आम नागरिकका लागि महँगो हुँदै जाने हो भने यो अभियानको उद्देश्य पूरा हुन सक्दैन। करिब ३५ लाख पुराना ब्रोडब्यान्ड ग्राहकको सेवा शुल्कमा भएको मूल्यवृद्धिको वास्तविक आधार सार्वजनिक नगरी नेपाल टेलिकमको सस्तो प्याकेज देखाएर मात्र सरकार आफ्नो जिम्मेवारीबाट मुक्त हुन सक्दैन। नयाँ उपकरणको मूल्य बढेको हो भने त्यसको पारदर्शी लागत नयाँ जडानमा देखाउन सकिन्छ। अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय ब्यान्डविथको लागत बढेको हो भने त्यसको प्रमाणित विवरण सार्वजनिक गर्न सकिन्छ। नेटवर्क सञ्चालन खर्च बढेको हो भने त्यसको तुलनात्मक अध्ययन गर्न सकिन्छ। तर यी सबैको वास्तविक आर्थिक प्रभाव नदेखाई लाखौँ पुराना ग्राहकको इन्टरनेट शुल्क एकैपटक बढाउनुको औचित्य सरकारले खोज्नैपर्छ। अब सरकारको प्राथमिकता निजी ISP हरूले मूल्य किन बढाए भन्ने प्रश्नको जवाफ खोज्नु, सम्भावित मूल्य मिलेमतोको छानबिन गर्नु र वास्तविक लागतका आधारमा उपभोक्तालाई न्यायोचित मूल्यमा इन्टरनेट उपलब्ध गराउनु हुनुपर्छ। सस्तो इन्टरनेटको प्रचारले मात्र डिजिटल नेपाल बन्दैन। पारदर्शी मूल्य, स्वस्थ प्रतिस्पर्धा, गुणस्तरीय सेवा र उपभोक्ताको अधिकार सुनिश्चित भएपछि मात्र डिजिटल नेपालको सपना साकार हुन्छ। Kathmandu. The recent price hikes in Nepal's internet service sector have added a serious financial burden to the common consumer. Public discontent has grown after private Internet Service Providers (ISPs) significantly increased their fees during Dashain. However, the government has not yet been able to provide an effective answer to the real reason for the price hike, how much it is related to costs, and the amount of additional financial burden on consumers. ISPAN, a joint organization of private internet service providers, has issued a public notice citing international circumstances as the reason for the price increase. He argues that the internet service fee has had to be increased, particularly due to the US-Iran war, the increase in petroleum prices in the international market, and the increase in the prices of fiber optic cables, routers, and other telecommunications equipment. However, an important question arises here - if the price of routers, fiber cables, and other equipment required to connect new customers has increased, why was the monthly fee of existing customers who have been using internet service for years increased all at once? Will the cost of operating internet services for millions of customers who are already connected increase in proportion to the increase in the price of petroleum products and fiber cables in the international market? Has the government studied the technical and economic basis for such arguments by private ISPs? Finding answers to these questions is a key responsibility of governments and regulatory bodies. Why were the fees for 3.5 million old customers increased? According to Nepal Telecommunications Authority (NTA) data, there are around 3.5 million fixed broadband internet subscribers in Nepal. These subscribers have been connected to the networks of various private ISPs for years. Fiber optic drop cables have been installed in their homes, offices and commercial establishments. Necessary routers and network equipment are also available. They are getting regular internet service from the networks extended through the poles of Nepal Telecom and Nepal Electricity Authority located on the roadside. The initial connection cost incurred when adding a new customer should be borne by the new customer. However, how fair is it to charge such a cost in addition to the regular internet service fee provided to customers already connected to the network? The silence of the regulatory body, the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, and the Nepal Telecommunication Authority on this issue has even raised suspicions of financial irregularities and collusion. Connecting a new customer may require additional investment in routers, drop cables, connectors, installation labor, and other equipment. But for existing customers, those equipment and installation costs have already been incurred. Therefore, the question naturally arises as to what is the justification for significantly increasing the monthly service fee of existing customers by citing the increased cost of new equipment. While continuing to provide service to existing customers, network maintenance, electricity, international bandwidth, network expansion, staff, and other operational costs will continue to be incurred. However, the extent to which these costs have increased and how much impact they will have on the customer's monthly fee must be proven through data. The price increase cannot be justified by putting the connection costs of new customers and the fees for regular bandwidth services provided to existing customers in the same basket. Why not allow new customers to choose their device options? As an immediate solution, the government can make arrangements to transparently separate fees for new connections and regular internet service. If a new customer wants to purchase a modern router, fiber drop cable, and other equipment as needed, they can be allowed to pay the actual cost separately. If the ISP is to provide the equipment, its price, quality, and ownership details should be clear. Similarly, in the case of old customers, a study should be conducted to determine whether the fees have been determined by adding the cost of equipment and infrastructure already connected to the new customer's connection cost. The government could, through a regulatory study, develop an option to maintain a reasonable differential between the service charges for existing customers and the equipment and infrastructure charges for new connections. This could give new customers the freedom to choose their equipment and help protect existing customers from unnecessary financial burdens. How much will war and rising oil prices increase internet charges? ISPs have also cited the US-Iran war and rising petroleum prices in the international market as reasons for raising fees. Of course, international wars, fuel price increases, transportation costs, foreign exchange rates, and equipment prices can all affect the costs of the telecommunications sector. But the question of how much their actual impact will be cannot be answered based on estimates. For example, if an ISP is serving millions of customers using fiber optic cables, routers, and other equipment that it has already purchased, there is no basis for all existing customers' monthly internet charges to automatically double if the international price of the new equipment increases. Similarly, actual changes in international bandwidth purchase prices, foreign currency exchange rates, electricity, network maintenance, and other operating costs should be accounted for separately. The government should publicize the true impact of international inflation by requesting comparative details of past and current costs from ISPs. Without verified details of the impact of the war, the cost of equipment, and the actual increase in operating costs, the burden of price increases cannot be passed on to the general consumer. What is the actual capacity of ISPs to sell packages of 100 to 600 Mbps? In the Nepali internet market, various service providers have announced packages of 100, 200, 300, 400, 600 Mbps and above. However, the article claims that the maximum speed of internet service in Nepal is only 88 Mbps. ISPs have also been accused of charging fees for local video content and even digital content stored on CDN servers connected to various locations in Nepal, by presenting it as international internet bandwidth. Why are the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology and the Nepal Telecommunication Authority silent on this issue? Customers are paying fees monthly, quarterly, semi-annually, and annually. But the general consumer is not aware of the relationship between the internet package purchased by the customer and the network capacity that the ISP can actually provide. Here comes another important technical topic - Oversubscription Ratio. This means how many customers the ISP has sold service to compared to the total available capacity of its network. Network operations are planned on the basis that not all customers use the maximum speed of their package at the same time. But the government should conduct a comparative study of each ISP's total purchased international bandwidth, local traffic, actual usage during peak hours, and capacity sold to customers. If an ISP has sold millions of customers various high-speed packages, what is the actual network capacity needed to serve those customers? How much speed are customers getting during peak hours? Has the service been sold beyond the capacity of the network? The answers to these questions should be made public through technical testing. Just because an internet package says 200 Mbps, it does not mean that the customer is always getting that speed. Therefore, the government should develop an effective monitoring system for independent speed tests, quality of service (QoS), and service level agreements (SLAs). The cost of content available through CDNs and the reality of international bandwidth should be made public. Nepal's major ISPs have been using Content Delivery Network (CDN) and local caching infrastructure from international content providers including Google, Meta, Netflix, and others. A CDN is a technology that places popular digital content on a network close to the customer, reducing the need to fetch content from an international internet gateway each time. In many cases, content providers provide their own caching equipment or facilitate the hosting of content within their network. In some cases, the ISP must bear the costs of infrastructure, electricity, network management, and connectivity. This doesn't mean that all CDN services are completely free, but it is important to note how much CDN and local traffic reduce the need for international bandwidth purchases. Therefore, the government should make the following data public: How much international bandwidth does each ISP purchase annually? How much does it cost per month to purchase international bandwidth? What percentage of total internet traffic is local traffic exchanged within Nepal? What proportion of content is available through CDN and caching infrastructure? What is the ratio of traffic coming from international gateways to local content traffic? How much has the ISP saved on international bandwidth costs by using local IXPs and CDNs? Only after these figures are made public can an objective debate be held about the true cost of internet service in Nepal. Why are cartel concerns about ISPs' price hikes? The fact that various private ISPs in Nepal increased internet fees at almost the same time has also raised questions about market competition. In a healthy competitive market, companies set prices based on their costs, investments, service quality, and business strategy. However, it is a matter of investigation when many competing companies increase prices of the same nature at the same time and try to justify it with the same types of reasons. Is this an independent business decision by all companies? Or is there some kind of price collusion in the market? Is the competition to provide cheaper services to consumers being weakened? The government should investigate these questions impartially. If evidence of possible price fixing or cartel is found, necessary action should be taken in accordance with prevailing competition laws. This issue needs to be investigated in coordination with the Nepal Telecommunications Authority, relevant competition regulatory bodies, and consumer rights bodies. The Minister of Communications should not show Nepal Telecom's cheap prices, but make the costs of private ISPs public. The details recently released by the Minister of Information and Communications Technology state that Nepal Telecom has seen a significant increase in subscribers to its fiber internet service, which has been provided at a subsidized rate since September 10. According to the minister, 11,764 new customers have been added from October 30 to November 16. Of these, 40 percent have opted for the concessionary rate package. Similarly, 28,192 people have registered for internet connection in the last three weeks. This initiative by Nepal Telecom is welcome. A government company providing cheap internet and competing with private companies is a positive thing for consumers. But there is another important statistic that the minister should make public - why did private ISPs increase internet prices? What is the real reason for that? Has the government studied the costs of private ISPs? At what price do they purchase international bandwidth? How much are they benefiting from CDN and local traffic? What is the economic basis for increasing service charges for existing customers? The government's role should not be limited to promoting Nepal Telecom's cheap packages. The private sector's pricing process should also be made transparent and accountable to provide relief to the common citizen from expensive internet. The government should form a high-level Internet cost study committee. The Government of Nepal should immediately form a high-level committee under the leadership of the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, comprising the Nepal Telecommunications Authority, independent telecommunications experts, economists, consumer rights activists, and relevant technical experts. The committee should study the actual operating costs, international bandwidth purchases, local traffic, CDN, network capacity, customer base, and revenue of Nepal's major ISPs. The real cost of bandwidth, especially in terms of gigabits per second (Mbps), should be a priority. The committee should study the following topics: 1. Actual purchase price and monthly cost of international bandwidth. 2. Ratio of local and international traffic. 3. Economic benefits from CDN and caching infrastructure. 4. Actual operating expenses and commercial profits of each ISP. 5. Package capacity sold to the customer and the actual available capacity of the network. 6. Difference between connection and service operation costs for old and new customers. 7. The actual internet speed and quality that the consumer receives according to the package purchased. 8. The impact of the recent price hike on consumers' monthly and annual spending. The study report should be made public and based on it, a clear policy regarding transparent pricing of internet services should be implemented. A transparent regulatory model similar to À La Carte implemented in pay TV is also needed for the Internet. The Government of Nepal has tried to regulate the services and prices offered by customers by implementing the À La Carte system in the television distribution business. Similarly, a transparent pricing system based on actual costs is also needed in the internet service sector. The government does not have to set the same price for all companies for internet access. However, a regulatory framework for pricing can be created based on minimum service quality, real costs, reasonable commercial returns, competition, and consumer rights. The Nepal Telecommunications Authority should conduct necessary studies within its jurisdiction in accordance with prevailing laws and make fee approval, price transparency, and service quality monitoring effective. The Internet is not a luxury item today. It is a basic infrastructure for education, health, banking, business, government services, employment, and communication. Therefore, the interests of the consumer should be given top priority in determining its price. The common citizen's clear questions to the government The government now needs to answer the following questions: 1. When will there be a fair investigation into the price hikes made by private ISPs at roughly the same time? 2. How much of a real impact have international wars and equipment price increases had on the monthly service charges of older customers? 3. Is the government ready to make public the ratio of international bandwidth purchases and local traffic of Nepal's major ISPs? 4. Why isn't there an independent test to see how much capacity or speed of International Internet Bandwidth customers who purchase 100, 200, 300, 400, and 600 Mbps packages are actually receiving? 5. Why not make a provision to assess separately the equipment and connection costs of new customers and the regular service charges of existing customers? 6. When will a transparent pricing system be implemented based on a study of the actual cost of internet on a per-gigabit basis? 7. It is public knowledge that the Inland Revenue Department has taken action in the past against ISPs for not paying the Telecommunication Service Charge (TSC) due to the Government of Nepal on time, issuing false bills and distorting billing records, and causing losses to the government in terms of TSC, and that the Supreme Court has upheld the action. This has also raised allegations that ISPs are trying to collect billions of rupees from ordinary Nepali consumers due to the government. In such a situation, when will there be an investigation into the Ministry of Communications, Nepal Telecommunications Authority, and the relevant ISPs, who are silently supporting the actions of ISPs without investigating them? Conclusion: If we are to create a digital Nepal, the internet should not be allowed to go beyond the reach of the people. The government is dreaming of a digital Nepal. But if the internet, which is considered the foundation of building a digital Nepal, becomes expensive for the common citizen, the objective of this campaign cannot be fulfilled. The government cannot absolve itself of its responsibility by simply showing Nepal Telecom's cheap packages without making public the real basis for the price hike in the service charges of about 3.5 million old broadband customers. If the price of new equipment has increased, its transparent cost can be shown in the new connection. If the cost of international bandwidth has increased, its verified details can be made public. If the cost of network operation has increased, a comparative study can be conducted. But the government must find the justification for increasing internet fees for millions of existing customers all at once without showing the real economic impact of all this. The government's priority now should be to find answers to the question of why private ISPs have increased prices, investigate possible price fixing, and provide internet to consumers at fair prices based on actual costs. Digital Nepal will not be achieved by promoting cheap internet alone. The dream of Digital Nepal will only be realized when transparent prices, healthy competition, quality services, and consumer rights are ensured.

के अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय बजारमा पेट्रोलियम पदार्थ र फाइबर केबलको मूल्य बढ्दैमा पहिले नै जडान भइसकेका लाखौँ ग्राहकको इन्टरनेट सेवा सञ्चालन लागत पनि त्यही अनुपातमा बढ्छ? सरकारले निजी ISP हरूको यस्तो तर्कको प्राविधिक र आर्थिक आधार अध्ययन गरेको छ कि छैन? यी प्रश्नको जवाफ खोज्नु सरकार र नियामक निकायको प्रमुख जिम्मेवारी हो। ३५ लाख पुराना ग्राहकको शुल्क किन बढाइयो ? नेपाल दूरसञ्चार प्राधिकरण (NTA) का तथ्यांकअनुसार नेपालमा फिक्स्ड ब्रोडब्यान्ड इन्टरनेटका ग्राहक करिब ३५ लाखको हाराहारीमा छन्। यी ग्राहक वर्षौंदेखि विभिन्न निजी ISP का नेटवर्कमा जोडिएका छन्। उनीहरूको घर, कार्यालय तथा व्यावसायिक प्रतिष्ठानमा फाइबर अप्टिक ड्रप केबल जडान भइसकेको छ। आवश्यक राउटर तथा नेटवर्क उपकरण पनि उपलब्ध छन्। सडक किनारमा रहेका नेपाल टेलिकम तथा नेपाल विद्युत् प्राधिकरणका पोलमार्फत विस्तार गरिएका नेटवर्कबाट उनीहरूले नियमित इन्टरनेट सेवा लिइरहेका छन्। नयाँ ग्राहक थप्दा लाग्ने प्रारम्भिक जडान खर्च नयाँ ग्राहकसँगै उठाउनुपर्ने हो। तर, पहिले नै नेटवर्कमा जोडिएका ग्राहकलाई दिइने नियमित इन्टरनेट सेवाको शुल्कमा समेत त्यस्तो खर्च जोडेर उठाउनु कति न्यायोचित हो? यस विषयमा नियामक निकाय, सञ्चार तथा सूचना प्रविधि मन्त्रालय र नेपाल दूरसञ्चार प्राधिकरणको मौनताले आर्थिक अनियमितता र मिलेमतोको आशंकासमेत बढाएको छ। नयाँ ग्राहक जडान गर्दा राउटर, ड्रप केबल, कनेक्टर, जडान श्रम तथा अन्य उपकरणमा अतिरिक्त लगानी आवश्यक पर्न सक्छ। तर पुराना ग्राहकका हकमा ती उपकरण र जडान खर्च पहिले नै भइसकेका हुन्छन्। त्यसैले नयाँ उपकरणको मूल्य बढेको कारण देखाएर पुराना ग्राहकको मासिक सेवा शुल्कसमेत उल्लेख्य रूपमा बढाउनुको औचित्य के हो भन्ने प्रश्न स्वाभाविक हो। पुराना ग्राहकलाई सेवा निरन्तर उपलब्ध गराउँदा नेटवर्क मर्मत, विद्युत्, अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय ब्यान्डविथ, नेटवर्क विस्तार, कर्मचारी तथा अन्य सञ्चालन खर्च भने लागिरहन्छन्। तर ती खर्चमा कति वृद्धि भयो र त्यसले ग्राहकको मासिक शुल्कमा कति प्रभाव पार्नुपर्ने हो भन्ने कुरा तथ्यांकबाट प्रमाणित हुनुपर्छ। नयाँ ग्राहकको जडान खर्च र पुराना ग्राहकलाई उपलब्ध गराइने नियमित ब्यान्डविथ सेवाको शुल्कलाई एउटै डालोमा राखेर मूल्यवृद्धिको औचित्य पुष्टि गर्न सकिँदैन। नयाँ ग्राहकले उपकरणको विकल्प रोज्न पाउने व्यवस्था किन नगर्ने ? निष्कर्ष : डिजिटल नेपाल बनाउने हो भने इन्टरनेट जनताको पहुँचभन्दा बाहिर जान दिनु हुँदैन सरकारले डिजिटल नेपालको सपना देखिरहेको छ। तर डिजिटल नेपाल निर्माणको आधार मानिने इन्टरनेट नै आम नागरिकका लागि महँगो हुँदै जाने हो भने यो अभियानको उद्देश्य पूरा हुन सक्दैन। करिब ३५ लाख पुराना ब्रोडब्यान्ड ग्राहकको सेवा शुल्कमा भएको मूल्यवृद्धिको वास्तविक आधार सार्वजनिक नगरी नेपाल टेलिकमको सस्तो प्याकेज देखाएर मात्र सरकार आफ्नो जिम्मेवारीबाट मुक्त हुन सक्दैन। नयाँ उपकरणको मूल्य बढेको हो भने त्यसको पारदर्शी लागत नयाँ जडानमा देखाउन सकिन्छ। अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय ब्यान्डविथको लागत बढेको हो भने त्यसको प्रमाणित विवरण सार्वजनिक गर्न सकिन्छ। नेटवर्क सञ्चालन खर्च बढेको हो भने त्यसको तुलनात्मक अध्ययन गर्न सकिन्छ। तर यी सबैको वास्तविक आर्थिक प्रभाव नदेखाई लाखौँ पुराना ग्राहकको इन्टरनेट शुल्क एकैपटक बढाउनुको औचित्य सरकारले खोज्नैपर्छ। अब सरकारको प्राथमिकता निजी ISP हरूले मूल्य किन बढाए भन्ने प्रश्नको जवाफ खोज्नु, सम्भावित मूल्य मिलेमतोको छानबिन गर्नु र वास्तविक लागतका आधारमा उपभोक्तालाई न्यायोचित मूल्यमा इन्टरनेट उपलब्ध गराउनु हुनुपर्छ। सस्तो इन्टरनेटको प्रचारले मात्र डिजिटल नेपाल बन्दैन। पारदर्शी मूल्य, स्वस्थ प्रतिस्पर्धा, गुणस्तरीय सेवा र उपभोक्ताको अधिकार सुनिश्चित भएपछि मात्र डिजिटल नेपालको सपना साकार हुन्छ।

३५ लाख पुराना ग्राहकको शुल्क किन बढाइयो ?

मन्त्रीका अनुसार असोज ३० देखि कात्तिक १६ गतेसम्म ११ हजार ७६४ नयाँ ग्राहक थपिएका छन्। तीमध्ये ४० प्रतिशतले सहुलियत दरको प्याकेज रोजेका छन्। त्यसैगरी, पछिल्लो तीन सातामा २८ हजार १९२ जनाले इन्टरनेट जडानका लागि नाम टिपाएका छन्।

नेपाल टेलिकमको यो पहल स्वागतयोग्य छ। सरकारी कम्पनीले सस्तो इन्टरनेट उपलब्ध गराउनु र निजी कम्पनीसँग प्रतिस्पर्धा गर्नु उपभोक्ताका लागि सकारात्मक विषय हो।

तर मन्त्रीले सार्वजनिक गर्नुपर्ने अर्को महत्वपूर्ण तथ्यांक पनि छ- निजी ISP हरूले इन्टरनेटको मूल्य किन बढाए ? त्यसको वास्तविक कारण के हो ?

सरकारले निजी ISP हरूको लागत अध्ययन गरेको छ कि छैन ? उनीहरूले अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय ब्यान्डविथ कति मूल्यमा खरिद गर्छन् ? CDN र स्थानीय ट्राफिकबाट कति लाभ लिइरहेका छन् ? पुराना ग्राहकको सेवा शुल्क बढाउनुको आर्थिक आधार के हो ?

सरकारको भूमिका नेपाल टेलिकमको सस्तो प्याकेजको प्रचार गर्नुमा मात्र सीमित हुनुहुँदैन। आम नागरिकलाई महँगो इन्टरनेटबाट राहत दिन निजी क्षेत्रको मूल्य निर्धारण प्रक्रिया पनि पारदर्शी र जवाफदेही बनाउनुपर्छ।

सरकारले गठन गर्नुपर्छ उच्चस्तरीय इन्टरनेट लागत अध्ययन समिति

नेपाल सरकारले तत्काल सञ्चार तथा सूचना प्रविधि मन्त्रालयको नेतृत्वमा नेपाल दूरसञ्चार प्राधिकरण, स्वतन्त्र दूरसञ्चार विज्ञ, अर्थशास्त्री, उपभोक्ता अधिकारकर्मी तथा सम्बन्धित प्राविधिक विशेषज्ञ सम्मिलित उच्चस्तरीय समिति गठन गर्नुपर्छ ।

उक्त समितिले नेपालका प्रमुख ISP हरूको वास्तविक सञ्चालन लागत, अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय ब्यान्डविथ खरिद, स्थानीय ट्राफिक, CDN, नेटवर्क क्षमता, ग्राहक संख्या र आम्दानीको अध्ययन गर्नुपर्छ ।

विशेषगरी प्रतिमेगाबिट प्रतिसेकेन्ड (Mbps) का आधारमा ब्यान्डविथको वास्तविक लागत कति पर्छ भन्ने विषयलाई प्राथमिकतामा राखिनुपर्छ ।

समितिले निम्न विषयमा अध्ययन गर्नुपर्छ :

१. अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय ब्यान्डविथको वास्तविक खरिद मूल्य र प्रतिमहिना लागत।

२. स्थानीय तथा अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय ट्राफिकको अनुपात।

३. CDN तथा क्यासिङ पूर्वाधारबाट प्राप्त हुने आर्थिक लाभ।

४. प्रत्येक ISP को वास्तविक सञ्चालन खर्च र व्यावसायिक नाफा।

५. ग्राहकलाई बिक्री गरिएको प्याकेज क्षमता र नेटवर्कको वास्तविक उपलब्ध क्षमता।

६. पुराना र नयाँ ग्राहकको जडान तथा सेवा सञ्चालन लागतबीचको अन्तर।

७. उपभोक्ताले खरिद गरेको प्याकेजअनुसार प्राप्त गर्ने वास्तविक इन्टरनेट गति र गुणस्तर।

८. पछिल्लो मूल्यवृद्धिले उपभोक्ताको मासिक तथा वार्षिक खर्चमा पारेको प्रभाव।

अध्ययन प्रतिवेदन सार्वजनिक गरिनुपर्छ र त्यसका आधारमा इन्टरनेट सेवाको पारदर्शी मूल्य निर्धारणसम्बन्धी स्पष्ट नीति लागू गरिनुपर्छ।

पे-टिभीमा लागू भएको ÀLa Carte जस्तै पारदर्शी नियामकीय मोडल इन्टरनेटमा पनि आवश्यक

नेपाल सरकारले टेलिभिजन वितरण व्यवसायमा À La Carte प्रणाली लागू गरेर ग्राहकले लिने सेवा र त्यसको मूल्यलाई व्यवस्थित गर्ने प्रयास गरेको छ। त्यसैगरी, इन्टरनेट सेवा क्षेत्रमा पनि वास्तविक लागतमा आधारित पारदर्शी मूल्य निर्धारण प्रणाली आवश्यक छ।

सरकारले सबै कम्पनीका लागि इन्टरनेटको मूल्य एउटै तोक्नुपर्छ भन्ने होइन। तर न्यूनतम सेवा गुणस्तर, वास्तविक लागत, उचित व्यावसायिक प्रतिफल, प्रतिस्पर्धा र उपभोक्ता अधिकारलाई आधार बनाएर मूल्य निर्धारणको नियामकीय ढाँचा बनाउन सकिन्छ।

नेपाल दूरसञ्चार प्राधिकरणले प्रचलित कानुनअनुसार आफ्नो अधिकारक्षेत्रभित्र आवश्यक अध्ययन गरी शुल्क स्वीकृति, मूल्य पारदर्शिता तथा सेवा गुणस्तर अनुगमनलाई प्रभावकारी बनाउनुपर्छ।

इन्टरनेट आज विलासिताको वस्तु होइन। शिक्षा, स्वास्थ्य, बैंकिङ, व्यापार, सरकारी सेवा, रोजगारी र सञ्चारको आधारभूत पूर्वाधार हो। त्यसैले यसको मूल्य निर्धारणमा उपभोक्ताको हितलाई सर्वोच्च प्राथमिकता दिनुपर्छ।

सरकारसँग आम नागरिकका स्पष्ट प्रश्न

अब सरकारले निम्न प्रश्नको जवाफ दिन आवश्यक छ :

१. निजी ISP हरूले लगभग एकै समयमा गरेको मूल्यवृद्धिको निष्पक्ष छानबिन कहिले हुन्छ?

२. अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय युद्ध र उपकरणको मूल्यवृद्धिले पुराना ग्राहकको मासिक सेवा शुल्कमा कति वास्तविक प्रभाव पारेको छ?

३. नेपालका प्रमुख ISP हरूको अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय ब्यान्डविथ खरिद र स्थानीय ट्राफिकको अनुपात सार्वजनिक गर्न सरकार तयार छ?

४. १००, २००, ३००, ४०० र ६०० Mbps का प्याकेज खरिद गर्ने ग्राहकले वास्तविक रूपमा कति क्षमता वा गतिको International Internet Bandwidth प्राप्त गरिरहेका छन् भन्ने स्वतन्त्र परीक्षण किन हुँदैन?

५. नयाँ ग्राहकको उपकरण तथा जडान खर्च र पुराना ग्राहकको नियमित सेवा शुल्कलाई छुट्टाछुट्टै मूल्यांकन गर्ने व्यवस्था किन नगर्ने?

६. इन्टरनेटको वास्तविक लागत प्रतिमेगाबिटका आधारमा अध्ययन गरी पारदर्शी मूल्य निर्धारण प्रणाली कहिले लागू हुन्छ?

७. विगतमा ISP हरूले नेपाल सरकारलाई बुझाउनुपर्ने Telecommunication Service Charge (TSC) अर्थात् दूरसञ्चार सेवा दस्तुर समयमै नबुझाएको, झुटो बिल–बिजक जारी गरी बिलिङ रेकर्ड तोडमोड गरेर सरकारलाई TSC मा हानि–नोक्सानी पुर्‍याएको विषयमा आन्तरिक राजस्व विभागले कारबाही गरेको र उक्त कारबाही प्रक्रियालाई सर्वोच्च अदालतले सदर गरेको विषय सार्वजनिक छ।

त्यसबाट ISP हरूले सरकारलाई बुझाउनुपर्ने अर्बौं रकम सोझासाझा नेपाली उपभोक्ताबाट उठाउन खोजेको आरोपसमेत उठेको छ। यस्तो अवस्थामा ISP हरूको कार्यमाथि छानबिन नगरी मौन समर्थन गरिरहेको सञ्चार मन्त्रालय, नेपाल दूरसञ्चार प्राधिकरण तथा सम्बन्धित ISP हरूमाथि छानबिन कहिले हुन्छ?

निष्कर्ष : डिजिटल नेपाल बनाउने हो भने इन्टरनेट जनताको पहुँचभन्दा बाहिर जान दिनु हुँदैन

सरकारले डिजिटल नेपालको सपना देखिरहेको छ। तर डिजिटल नेपाल निर्माणको आधार मानिने इन्टरनेट नै आम नागरिकका लागि महँगो हुँदै जाने हो भने यो अभियानको उद्देश्य पूरा हुन सक्दैन।

करिब ३५ लाख पुराना ब्रोडब्यान्ड ग्राहकको सेवा शुल्कमा भएको मूल्यवृद्धिको वास्तविक आधार सार्वजनिक नगरी नेपाल टेलिकमको सस्तो प्याकेज देखाएर मात्र सरकार आफ्नो जिम्मेवारीबाट मुक्त हुन सक्दैन।

नयाँ उपकरणको मूल्य बढेको हो भने त्यसको पारदर्शी लागत नयाँ जडानमा देखाउन सकिन्छ। अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय ब्यान्डविथको लागत बढेको हो भने त्यसको प्रमाणित विवरण सार्वजनिक गर्न सकिन्छ। नेटवर्क सञ्चालन खर्च बढेको हो भने त्यसको तुलनात्मक अध्ययन गर्न सकिन्छ।

तर यी सबैको वास्तविक आर्थिक प्रभाव नदेखाई लाखौँ पुराना ग्राहकको इन्टरनेट शुल्क एकैपटक बढाउनुको औचित्य सरकारले खोज्नैपर्छ।

अब सरकारको प्राथमिकता निजी ISP हरूले मूल्य किन बढाए भन्ने प्रश्नको जवाफ खोज्नु, सम्भावित मूल्य मिलेमतोको छानबिन गर्नु र वास्तविक लागतका आधारमा उपभोक्तालाई न्यायोचित मूल्यमा इन्टरनेट उपलब्ध गराउनु हुनुपर्छ।

सस्तो इन्टरनेटको प्रचारले मात्र डिजिटल नेपाल बन्दैन। पारदर्शी मूल्य, स्वस्थ प्रतिस्पर्धा, गुणस्तरीय सेवा र उपभोक्ताको अधिकार सुनिश्चित भएपछि मात्र डिजिटल नेपालको सपना साकार हुन्छ।

Kathmandu. The recent price hikes in Nepal's internet service sector have added a serious financial burden to the common consumer. Public discontent has grown after private Internet Service Providers (ISPs) significantly increased their fees during Dashain. However, the government has not yet been able to provide an effective answer to the real reason for the price hike, how much it is related to costs, and the amount of additional financial burden on consumers. ISPAN, a joint organization of private internet service providers, has issued a public notice citing international circumstances as the reason for the price increase. He argues that the internet service fee has had to be increased, particularly due to the US-Iran war, the increase in petroleum prices in the international market, and the increase in the prices of fiber optic cables, routers, and other telecommunications equipment. However, an important question arises here - if the price of routers, fiber cables, and other equipment required to connect new customers has increased, why was the monthly fee of existing customers who have been using internet service for years increased all at once? Will the cost of operating internet services for millions of customers who are already connected increase in proportion to the increase in the price of petroleum products and fiber cables in the international market? Has the government studied the technical and economic basis for such arguments by private ISPs? Finding answers to these questions is a key responsibility of governments and regulatory bodies. Why were the fees for 3.5 million old customers increased? According to Nepal Telecommunications Authority (NTA) data, there are around 3.5 million fixed broadband internet subscribers in Nepal. These subscribers have been connected to the networks of various private ISPs for years. Fiber optic drop cables have been installed in their homes, offices and commercial establishments. Necessary routers and network equipment are also available. They are getting regular internet service from the networks extended through the poles of Nepal Telecom and Nepal Electricity Authority located on the roadside. The initial connection cost incurred when adding a new customer should be borne by the new customer. However, how fair is it to charge such a cost in addition to the regular internet service fee provided to customers already connected to the network? The silence of the regulatory body, the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, and the Nepal Telecommunication Authority on this issue has even raised suspicions of financial irregularities and collusion. Connecting a new customer may require additional investment in routers, drop cables, connectors, installation labor, and other equipment. But for existing customers, those equipment and installation costs have already been incurred. Therefore, the question naturally arises as to what is the justification for significantly increasing the monthly service fee of existing customers by citing the increased cost of new equipment. While continuing to provide service to existing customers, network maintenance, electricity, international bandwidth, network expansion, staff, and other operational costs will continue to be incurred. However, the extent to which these costs have increased and how much impact they will have on the customer's monthly fee must be proven through data. The price increase cannot be justified by putting the connection costs of new customers and the fees for regular bandwidth services provided to existing customers in the same basket. Why not allow new customers to choose their device options? As an immediate solution, the government can make arrangements to transparently separate fees for new connections and regular internet service. If a new customer wants to purchase a modern router, fiber drop cable, and other equipment as needed, they can be allowed to pay the actual cost separately. If the ISP is to provide the equipment, its price, quality, and ownership details should be clear. Similarly, in the case of old customers, a study should be conducted to determine whether the fees have been determined by adding the cost of equipment and infrastructure already connected to the new customer's connection cost. The government could, through a regulatory study, develop an option to maintain a reasonable differential between the service charges for existing customers and the equipment and infrastructure charges for new connections. This could give new customers the freedom to choose their equipment and help protect existing customers from unnecessary financial burdens. How much will war and rising oil prices increase internet charges? ISPs have also cited the US-Iran war and rising petroleum prices in the international market as reasons for raising fees. Of course, international wars, fuel price increases, transportation costs, foreign exchange rates, and equipment prices can all affect the costs of the telecommunications sector. But the question of how much their actual impact will be cannot be answered based on estimates. For example, if an ISP is serving millions of customers using fiber optic cables, routers, and other equipment that it has already purchased, there is no basis for all existing customers' monthly internet charges to automatically double if the international price of the new equipment increases. Similarly, actual changes in international bandwidth purchase prices, foreign currency exchange rates, electricity, network maintenance, and other operating costs should be accounted for separately. The government should publicize the true impact of international inflation by requesting comparative details of past and current costs from ISPs. Without verified details of the impact of the war, the cost of equipment, and the actual increase in operating costs, the burden of price increases cannot be passed on to the general consumer. What is the actual capacity of ISPs to sell packages of 100 to 600 Mbps? In the Nepali internet market, various service providers have announced packages of 100, 200, 300, 400, 600 Mbps and above. However, the article claims that the maximum speed of internet service in Nepal is only 88 Mbps. ISPs have also been accused of charging fees for local video content and even digital content stored on CDN servers connected to various locations in Nepal, by presenting it as international internet bandwidth. Why are the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology and the Nepal Telecommunication Authority silent on this issue? Customers are paying fees monthly, quarterly, semi-annually, and annually. But the general consumer is not aware of the relationship between the internet package purchased by the customer and the network capacity that the ISP can actually provide. Here comes another important technical topic - Oversubscription Ratio. This means how many customers the ISP has sold service to compared to the total available capacity of its network. Network operations are planned on the basis that not all customers use the maximum speed of their package at the same time. But the government should conduct a comparative study of each ISP's total purchased international bandwidth, local traffic, actual usage during peak hours, and capacity sold to customers. If an ISP has sold millions of customers various high-speed packages, what is the actual network capacity needed to serve those customers? How much speed are customers getting during peak hours? Has the service been sold beyond the capacity of the network? The answers to these questions should be made public through technical testing. Just because an internet package says 200 Mbps, it does not mean that the customer is always getting that speed. Therefore, the government should develop an effective monitoring system for independent speed tests, quality of service (QoS), and service level agreements (SLAs). The cost of content available through CDNs and the reality of international bandwidth should be made public. Nepal's major ISPs have been using Content Delivery Network (CDN) and local caching infrastructure from international content providers including Google, Meta, Netflix, and others. A CDN is a technology that places popular digital content on a network close to the customer, reducing the need to fetch content from an international internet gateway each time. In many cases, content providers provide their own caching equipment or facilitate the hosting of content within their network. In some cases, the ISP must bear the costs of infrastructure, electricity, network management, and connectivity. This doesn't mean that all CDN services are completely free, but it is important to note how much CDN and local traffic reduce the need for international bandwidth purchases.
